utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted to respond very quickly to a communication from Mr. Robinson that I believe the Court is aware of concerning scheduling for the upcoming week that was sent on the 23rd at about 5.30. In any event, if just to remind the Court, this referred to the Defence inability to cross-examine a particular -- have a particular witness called, in short. And basically I wanted to endorse Mr. Robinson's communication. The Court will certainly be aware of the prodigious efforts, behind-the-scene efforts by the Prosecution to ensure that the schedule proceeds seamlessly. In this case, we had a witness who was unable to appear before Easter. That was the next witness in order and so we undertook every effort possible to fill the schedule. That obviously is made more difficult by the upcoming one-week break, which means that one of the priorities has to be not having a witness remain for that period of time. I think everyone did their best. We're grateful for the Defence accommodation with respect to one of the witnesses and their willingness to have that witness called, and we completely understand the Defence position with respect to the other witness. I didn't think it was fair to allow that e-mail to sit out there alone without providing that kind of feedback. So I just wanted to let the Court know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. While we're discussing some administrative matters, with the indulgence of the witness, if I can ask Mr. Robinson, since you informed us that the Defence is minded to present an oral submission for Rule 98 bis, then can I ask you how -- how long after the close of the Prosecution case you would need for its preparation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we could do it within one week of the final closing of the Prosecution's case, which would include any decision on outstanding motions so that we know what -- all of the evidence that the Prosecution have been allowed to make as part of its case. Within one week after that, we would be prepared to present our oral motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, if the witness could take the solemn declaration, please, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. May I go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, could the Chamber go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, madam. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Schmitz. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What is your name?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Christine Schmitz.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: My profession is nurse.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how long have you been a nurse?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, I did my exams in 1984.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Did you work for a non-governmental organisation in July of 1995 posted in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, could you bear in mind the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both of you are speaking the same language. Please put a pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 90323.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Ma'am, in front you, you'll see a piece of paper. It says amalgamated witness statement and your signature on the bottom. This statement was prepared containing relevant portions of two interviews that you gave to the OTP. One was in 1999; and one was last year. It also contains additional clarifications that you have recently given. Is this the statement that you signed on March 21st, last week?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, this is the statement I signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you confirm that this statement accurately reflects an amalgamation of your previous interviews and the information you previous -- just provided?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if you were asked today about the same matters in the statement, would you give substantially the same information?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the statement be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4752, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, there also are several associated exhibits but I would like to make a correction in regard to the last exhibit admitted on the table, which is 65 ter 31314D. We're not going to tender that. I will ask her about it and just ask that it be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we deal with the associated exhibit, in-chief examination is over. You are not going to ask any questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to ask some questions. However, if I had a sense as to the Trial Chamber's position on the associated exhibits, I might ask less questions. But I'm certainly prepared to deal with it at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, if I can read a very short summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, for the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Christine Schmitz is a nurse who began working in the Srebrenica hospital in late June 1995. She was present in the town of Srebrenica when the attack started on 6 July. On the 11th, she and her colleagues evacuated to Potocari where she reported a lack of water and food for the refugees. On the 12th and 13th, she witnessed the deportation of the refugees and the separations of the Muslim males. Ms. Schmitz was present at a meeting on the 15th with the VRS and Bosnian Serb representatives where the evacuation of patients, staff, including the local staff, was discussed. Her patients were evacuated on 17th, and on the 21st, she left Potocari along with the Dutch and UN Military Observers. However, not all of her local male staff made it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Ms. Schmitz, I'm just going to have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if I can have 65 ter 23109. And this is in e-court page 59.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, Ms. Schmitz, for you, this is July 15th, and it's ending in 6193.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'll just put on the record that the witness has her documents in front of her in hard copy for ease of reference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, ma'am, in front of us we have a document, it's hard to read but it's the 15th of July. Do you recognise what form of document this is?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes. This is A telex I had sent to the team that Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And on the 15th July is this a period of time when you were in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, in the beginning of this document it says: "Nikolic was just here in order to arrange a meeting for tonight with the UN and senior officers of the BSA." And then on the agenda we have three items: One, evacuation of wounded; two, local staff; three, leaving of UNPROFOR. Can you tell us about number two, what was the discussion expected to be about the local staff?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, there was still eight local staff members with us, with Daniel and me - Daniel was my Australian colleague - and seven of the eight were young male staff, and one female translator. They stayed with us in the UN compound in Potocari, and given that the population had been deported and the male Bosnian population been separated, we didn't know what would happen to them. So the discussion was supposed to be -- or my agenda was that I wanted to take the national staff with us out of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this would include those males that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes. Especially.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd move to admit that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it one of the associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. There are several documents in the same number.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can take a moment to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: There is one 65 ter number, 23109. There are several documents associated with that number. That's a chronological order -- ordering of the witness's telexes that she sent out during the relevant period of time. In addition to that, on the table, you will find occasions where in the amalgamated statement she was asked about specific documents within that section and we've delineated those specifically for you, but it will be my intention to ask for the admission of the entire exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On a technical issue why do I see a document that says: "Document to be used in private session and tendered under seal." I can't -- I can't see the content on my personal computer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think that could be a mistake as to the beginning of the front -- cover page of this document. These documents will not be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Uh-huh. What's the page number of this document, what we just saw?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: E-court 59. And for the actual page number, on the right-hand corner, it is R0106193.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are tendering the entire document or only this page?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I would like, at the end, tender the entire document. I'm unclear as to how you would like me to proceed. I am going to go through at least ten of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you proceed and then let us consider whether to admit in its entirety or separately at the end of your examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have the same 65 ter number, number 65 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, ma'am, this is for you page number 6199. This is just the next day, July 16th. It's on the screen in front of you as well. In this telex it says: "In the meeting yesterday, a list with all names of local staff has been given to the BSA plus a number of patients in Potocari." Ma'am, the meeting that this refers to, is this the meeting that you had on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you tell us about the list that was given?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, the list had been prepared by one of the colleagues of that national team, and I had given it to the BSA in that meeting. I certainly did not have the list of the 45 patients in Bratunac because these patients were - how to say this? - the list was with the UN. I had no knowledge about or not much knowledge about what was happening to them and so on. So that list was not given by me but by the UN.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And let's focus for a moment about the list that contains just the names of the local staff. And that list, is that a list that you gave to the VRS and the BSA authorities on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to move to e-court page 66. And in hard copy, this is 6200. This is also from the 16th. And is this another telex that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, this is another telex.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. If we go down to about the middle it says: "Please confirm again my thoughts: MSF will stay if our local staff cannot be included in the convoy and leave then later with the local staff." Ma'am, on the 16th, what the was your intention regarding whether to stay or go and how the local staff played in that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, I thought always that Daniel, myself, and the national staff remaining with us, we would leave with the convoy of the patients. So the convoy of the patients was planned for the 17th, and I was still of the intention to go with the national staff on that convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And the next sentence is: "According to UNPROFOR we can go together, but you never know. Every local staff has an MSF shirt/west and is identified with ID with their job they have in MSF." Here it talks about an identification card for the local staff. Can you tell us about that process? Did all local staff receive an identification card?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, when I arrived in Srebrenica, people had that already, so I wouldn't be able today to confirm that everybody had one, and I remember in one of the other telexes it is being said that one guy had lost it. But so normally, yes, national staff with MSF does have an ID card if is a well-settled programme. Maybe not in the first days of an emergency.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. If we go down to the very bottom it says -- it's after your name, "XTINA," and then 3.50: [As read] "Please don't be disappointed: Just get informed by UN -- just got informed by UN: Mr. Deronjic Miroslav, special rep of Karadzic in Bratunac, called and informed that the convoy passed Zvornik and it was on its way to here. Five minutes later Tuzla called and informed us that the convoy has been shot at and had to return." This information, is this information that you received yourself or did you receive it from someone else?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I received it from somebody of the UN. What happened in Potocari is that there was always one of the soldiers running behind me if there was some news I was supposed to have from, for example, Commander Franken. So I wouldn't remember who that soldier was but he came to me and told me that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And regard to this name Miroslav Deronjic, special representative of Karadzic, at the time is this somebody that you knew?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to talk to you about little bit about the times here. We see before this it says 3.50 and then up top it says: "Hello Stephan and Belgrade team," and then it says 3.25. Tell us about these times and the process by which you wrote this.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, you do have on the telexes as well the time when it's being sent, but sometimes there was time in between. Sometimes I started to write and then something came in between and I sent it off later. But here that is a very good example. I started to write by 3.25, maybe that's my German pedantics, and then when I finished it I just wanted to send it off. And you can see here 3.50, then this information came and I just put it at the end behind my name, and four minutes later I sent it off.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And so this information at the very bottom, is this information that you typed in almost directly after you received it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this process by which you were typing your telexes -- strike that. When you received information that you thought was important to go into a telex, how much time passed before you actually wrote the telex?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: This cannot be answered in terms of every half an hour after news came up I wrote a telex because I balanced it with my other tasks. So my principle was as quick as possible, because I knew that Belgrade needed the information. But, again, for example, when a situation happens where wounded are included, I wouldn't first write a telex and then take care for the wounded but the other way around. So as close to the event when things happened I wrote, but not always immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I know you've had an opportunity to look at all the telexes that are referenced in your amalgamated statement. Is that -- does that process apply to all of them?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're now going to look at 65 ter 23111. And --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: What was the number for me?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 65 ter 23111. You will see it on the screen in front of you shortly.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a listing of several names, and some of the names in it have circles around them. Can you tell us about this document and about the events that produced this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you proceed, could you take a look at the LiveNote and there's request from the interpreters and court reporters. Please be slow or put a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Schmitz.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you kindly repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. The document we see in front of us, for example, number 3 has a circle around it. Can you tell us about the events surrounding this document and that circle?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Okay. So this document is the document of the patients who were on the 17th of July present in Potocari under our care. When it became clear that ICRC, the International Committee of the Red Cross, would evacuate the patients on 17th, Commander Nikolic of BSA wanted to inspect all the patients in the UN compound. The list had been prepared not by myself personally but one of my national colleagues, and so whilst Commander Nikolic was going around the little hospital where the patients were laying, I circled seven names of seven male patients. And these seven male patients were supposed to remain with the Ministry of Health in Bratunac and were not allowed to continue with ICRC to Tuzla because they were supposed to be war criminals. So that's the reason why I circled them. I need one moment ... I believe because number 3 is circled but then scratched, that this one was -- he was not among them. You will find seven clearly marked names after.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Schmitz, you called -- you said Commander Nikolic. So you understood him at the time to be a commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we go to page 10. E-court page 10 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And it's the last page of this document. And this is notes, handwritten notes, and they appear to be on the back page, and in the middle we have: "Meeting Nikolic, July 17th, 1.00. Civil affairs commissioner." Please tell us about this meeting.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: That was one of the two meetings on that day with members of BSA. So that meeting was with Commander Nikolic and the commissioner of civil affairs whose name I don't know. And basically it refers to the telex we had spoken a bit earlier about, where the convoy had been shot at. And here I note down that we should accept the apologies about that event, and that Commander Franken of UNPROFOR would not accept the selection inquiry of the patients which happened any way, afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Right before this -- excuse me. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: So in this meeting, also it was said that the local staff of MSF had been amnestied.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We'll get to that in one moment. But I just want to back up for a moment. Before this document we looked at your document from July 16th. We don't have to go back there. But this was the document where you talked about the addition at 3.50, Miroslav Deronjic special rep of Mr. Karadzic had called. Did you understand that that Miroslav Deronjic was this same person that you met on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Today for me it would be only logical but I do not remember that at that time I realised that is the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 23132.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, ma'am, you're just going to see this on the screen. I think that will be easier. This is July 17th, the same day as this meeting. And here it says: "Just coming from a meeting with Nikolic and the commissioner of Bratunac." If we go down it says: "All local staff will be [sic] amnestied." Is this what you were referring to a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, at that time, it was only important for me. I didn't know what it meant, amnestied. But I understood it that the national staff could remain with us and leave with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: As opposed to doing what?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: As opposed to have to let them go and let them separated by BSA or whatever, but the fate of the other men in Potocari. Do I say this clearly enough? Well, basically my worry was that the male national staff would be killed, and this is what I wanted to prevent. And by getting informed that they were amnestied, I understood that they wouldn't be killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to go to 65 ter 23109. E-court page 68. And you can just see it in front of you if that's easier. This is -- we're backing up a day, but this is July 16th. This is e-court page 68 of 65 ter 23109. Thank you. All right. This document says: "Hello, Stephan." Tell us who Stephan is?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Stephan, actually, that's the name -- the way I called it. He was our head of mission in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And down the document it says: "Here, follow the names of our local staff." And then it's a listing of eight names. Did you put these names in this telex?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did put the names in the telex. I did not put the list together because I didn't have the time for that. I believe that one of the national staff put it together.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 31314D. And we'll need page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this is an intercept from July 19th. And starting on page 3, I'm going to read through this and then ask you questions as we go. It says: "Is this Jankovic? "Speaking. "Hello. "Speaking. "Colonel Djurdjic speaking. "I'm listening. "Janko? "Yes. "Is that you? "Yes, it's me. "We should talk but I've got to make an effort to hear you. "Okay. "Regarding what you were asking? "Yes. "The boss has ordered that they be halted. "Yes. "This is what he wrote. "Yes. "That Christina" - I think it's Schmitz - "the nurse can go." So obviously is this a reference to you.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And Daniel O'Brien. Can you tell us who Daniel O'Brien is?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: That was my Australian colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I'll continue: "Yes. "The physician." Was he a physician?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yeah, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I'll continue: "Can you hear me well? "Yes." And this is the next page -- yes, apologies. "You hear me well? "I can hear you. "And only women and children can go. Understand? "And what about those young men? "Others ... I don't know, they might require the whole group to go. "Say again? "That they will require, but they have government's permission for all of them to go. "God-damn it, can we do this conversation through the girl? I have to ask her to act as a mediator here ..." I'll stop there for a moment. Were there occasions where you did act as a mediator for people from the BSA?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Mediating between BSA and whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Strike that. Let me ask another question. Were there occasions where you had negotiations with the BSA regarding issues?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We'll continue. "Listen. "Yes. "So, they have permission from ... the Koljevic government? "Yes. "That they can all go. They have a list." I'm going to stop there. What follows is a list of names. And I want you to follow this list of names but I'm going to read out the list of names from 65 ter 23109, e-court page 68, from a few days before, a telex we just looked at, and I'm going to ask you whether I read the list of names from your telex follows this intercept. So the first name that I have from your telex is Abdulah Perkovic. The second name I have is Ibrahim Ibramovic [phoen]. The third name is Muhidin Husic. Then I have Muhamed Masic, Sahin Talovic, Hajrudin Kurtic, and Omer Talovic. First of all, do you recognise those names?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And who are those people?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: This is the male local staff. Only the first surname of Abdulah, Abdulah the cook, is not correctly written.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll just continue a bit more on this intercept. It says: "They are taking them as local staff and they have permission from Karadz ..." and it stops and it says "Koljevic." "All right, they have permission but you know that the procedure you too took part in? "Great. "Pardon? "Great, if that's your position, it's good. The procedure is such, god-damned it, that it should be checked whether those --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We better have the English one for the benefit of the interpreters and court reporter. It disappeared. Bottom part.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I'm just going to have a few more sentences, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at the bottom here: "The procedure is such, god-damned it, that it should be checked whether those ... are they able-bodied or older than 60." So my question for you, ma'am, these male local staff who worked for your organisation, were they able-bodied men? Were they not very young and not very old, were they somewhere in the middle?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, they was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to go to 65 ter 23135. This is dated July 20th.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At the bottom of this telex the last sentence is -- I think it says: "Two male translators of our staff have disappeared before the evacuation. Meho apparently has been taken out of the buses." Can you tell us who Meho was?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Meho was our eighth male national staff. He was a logistician and sanitation staff member, and he had been suspended from work by the local opstina before I arrived on the 24th of June. So I had met him only once before the bombing started, during the distribution of hygienic passes as an incentive. On the 13th of July, I met him in the crowd of displaced population outside of the UN compound, and I asked him if he would want to come with us or I requested that he would come with us, because we needed help in the UN compound with the sanitation, but more important for me also I had wanted to keep him with us for his security because I was worried. But he decided to stay with his family.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when he stayed with his family on the 13th, is this on the -- outside of the compound at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 4459B. May I also request assistance from an usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: In the meantime, Ms. Schmitz, you're using the phrase "national staff" and "local staff." Are they being used interchangeably?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So now we're looking at 65 ter 4459B, which is an identification card. For the record we have just had the actual identification card handed to you. Are you holding that now?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I'm holding it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you recognise this card?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, it's a typical MSF ID card. And due to the time, since it was 1995, it is still the old logo. MSF has a new logo developed after that. But yes, this is an MSF ID card.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you recognise the person in the picture?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Can you turn the card over as well just so you see the back. Is this the type of ID card that local staff were using during July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 23109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Except for the telex I propose to deal with the exhibit when we are dealing with it. First, the intercept we saw, I noted that should be put under seal because I see some name of place in the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P4753, under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And why is this ID card relevant, Ms. West, if you could tell us?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We -- you have received information already that this was an identification card that was found in one of the graves. It was, I believe, in the Manning report. This is an ID card that she's indicated is the type of ID card that was used by her staff in July of 1995. She does not recognise the picture, but the information in the Manning report would identify the person as Meho Bosnjakovic - I'll get the spelling for you - and that is the individual in her staff who she just spoke about who would not come within the compound and who left on the one of the buses. This was found in a grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is the ID card that was found in that grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4754, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I have just one more document. 65 ter 23109, e-court page 40.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is July 12th. And this is late in the afternoon. This is almost 6.00. Ma'am, do you remember the events of July 12th, what happened on July 12th?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, what happened on July 12th is that, in short, the deportation of the population started around noon. In the morning until 10, there was supposed to be a kind of cease-fire or ultimatum so it was relatively quiet. Then quite a big number of buses and trucks arrived and the deportation of women and children and old people started. And I understood that there were no men on the buses. I didn't see them either. I'm sorry, maybe questions can be more defined because there was so much happening on that day that I -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'll ask you another question. During the day on July 12th, were you inside the compound or outside the compound?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Both. I -- in -- in the early afternoon I went back and forth between the compound and the big group of displaced, in order to see if there were sick or wounded or dehydrated children among the displaced, or people who were too old to cope, so I did bring them by myself in a pick-up back into the compound into Daniel's care in the little hospital in the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And after you would do that once, did you then go outside again to find more people?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you tell us generally what the state of the people were on the outside?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, people who were outside had already spent one night outside, had hardly anything to eat, little food. They had brought whilst fleeing on the 11th from Srebrenica to Potocari little water. There was a water truck who had been sent from Bratunac. People in general were shivering, not due to the temperature - it was extremely hot - but they were so fearful. And the children were just laying on the ground, very apathic, not playing, not crying. So, in short, people were horrified and -- so the condition was very difficult for them to cope and they didn't know what would go and happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in this telex you say: [As read] "We can hardly cope anymore. I have no strength anymore. It is so difficult to stay in contact with you. Please ask clearance for expatriates to take over from us." Can you tell us what your state of mind was at the time that you wrote this?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, in the early evening, I felt like I was cracking and I couldn't cope anymore. My heart was racing -- I'm sorry. And I felt I couldn't do my work anymore. I couldn't take care as much as I should have done anymore, so, therefore, I wrote that telex. And, of course, realising after that telex that it is not possible to be replaced but by just having said "I can't anymore," it was okay. So then I lay down for some time and I rested a bit and then it was okay. Then I could continue. But that was for me the deepest point of exhaustion where I just could not cope with the situation anymore, but then I went back to my normal strength and just continuing with what I thought was the right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, if you could take a look at para 24 and 25 of Ms. Schmitz's statement, here you present a bunch of documents with -- in relation to which Ms. Schmitz says that: "I have recently reviewed the documents and they are consistent with my memory of the events at the time." The problem the Chamber has is it -- it's difficult for -- of course, that they may speak for themselves, but the Chamber finds it difficult to find how relevant or -- they are and how they relate to the Prosecution case. So I found it very useful that you dealt with several documents in 23109 or some other documents here. Otherwise, the Chamber has some difficulty. It would be much better than if you tender by bar table motion because there you deal with such -- such issues. But I would like to hear from the Defence, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we would prefer the Chamber to stick with its previous practice with respect to admitting documents that are an indispensable part of the statement or that are referred to in court as opposed to admitting documents en masse. So that is our position in principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you prepared to deal with more documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm not, Your Honour, and I understand the Court's position. But I would ask for the admission of the specific documents I addressed with the witness but for the one that is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I lost track of the 65 ter numbers. Shall I leave it to the Registrar, in consultation with the parties --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- to identify and admit them in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate it. Thank you. Ma'am, are you all right? Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As you noted, your evidence in-chief was primarily admitted in form -- in the form of documents, i.e., in lieu of your oral testimony. And then you will now be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. But before -- before that, shall we move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, we are now in open session. Please start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Schmitz.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you the following: How many local staff members did you have working for you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: We did have 13 local staff working for us who were basically important for the functioning of the mission, like a driver or a cook. We did not consider the staff in the hospital as our staff, but it was the staff of the Ministry of Health.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the staff from the Ministry of Health of the Muslim part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the government in Sarajevo, when you say "staff from the Ministry of Health," these are the people you are referring to? This is the body you are referring to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: The staff of the hospital in Srebrenica I'm referring to is the staff of the Ministry of Health of Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know all of these 13 staff members?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No -- well, yes. I knew the 13 staff members, but as I said earlier, Meho I didn't know very well because he had been suspended and I met him only very briefly once. The other staff I did not know very well since I only arrived on 24th of June. That were just 12 days before the bombing on the 6th started. I'm saying it like this because after the 6th, I had much contact with few staff members, like Mohammed, the logistician, or the drivers, but I wouldn't remember, for example, the names of the cleaners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So could you tell us the reason for which Meho was suspended?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, it was Meho and Mohammed who had been suspended before my arrival. What happened is that the opstina, I believe in May, had issued the suspension because they said that Mohammed Masic, our logistician, should go back to school - he was a teacher before - and that others should have the opportunity as well to have the job. The unemployment in the enclave was very high, and we were ones of the few who were offering jobs. So my predecessor, Catherine, who I don't remember the surname, she did not agree with that because our experienced national staff is the background bone of the organisation so we didn't want to let them go. And so, as a reaction, she stopped the activities in the ambulantas around the town. So for that -- I call it conflict, Mohammed and Meho were suspended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did not recognise Meho on this identity document.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that begs the question if it was possible to forge your IDs.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But those IDs were obviously effective. They were useful because people respected them; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: What would you mean with "respected them"? It meant that this very person was a staff member of MSF.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And why did they need them?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: It's a usual procedure within MSF and its employment principles that a national staff member does have an ID. So, for example, if a driver is transporting a patient and crossing a check-point, he can identify himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I meant. Those IDs of yours were respected at the check-points; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: If you refer to the situation in Srebrenica, the drivers were not allowed to cross the check-point. I meant this as a principle example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But what were the IDs for, if not to be produced somewhere and in order to be able to pass?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, they were, for example, in Srebrenica, supposed to be able to be identified as a staff member in the city itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's leave it with that. You mentioned in your statements and in today's testimony two terms: Deportation and evacuation. Are you familiar with the legal implications of both terms?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No, I'm not sufficiently familiar with it. And I realised, when going through the documents, that I used them - how do you say this? - interchangeable. I never used the word "deportation" for the evacuation of the patients on the 17th of July. I did apply the word "deportation" on the deportation of the population on 12th and 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But without any prejudice as to the legal implications; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Would you please explain me the word "prejudice"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I would like to know is whether you were selective in your choice of terms based on the legal meaning of the term. You probably used these terms spontaneously without taking into account the legal implications.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I used the words and the definition as much as I knew them. I'm not claiming to know the legal implications up to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On pages 15 and 16 of today's transcript, you are recorded to have said that you knew about the fate of the people in Potocari and that you wanted to prevent that those you wanted to protect meet a similar fate. What did you know about the fate of the people in Potocari on that day?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, would you please repeat on which page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's our transcript today. You can't scroll back. It's on your monitor. So could you be more specific -- could you repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If convenient, I can read it out. I can read out the answers to the questions. Just a minute. Here it is. The question was -- it is about abolition. [In English] "... all local staff ... will be amnestied" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Karadzic, I noted the translation issue again. It was translated as "abolished," but if I remember correctly it should be translated "pardoned" or "amnestied" of local staff. So while you're dealing with those local staff, you said this. I will read it out: "... as opposed to have to let them go and let them separated by BSA or whatever, but the fate of the other men in Potocari." Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He was referring to that fate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you know then about the fate of the people at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, I knew that the men were not allowed to go with their families, their mothers, wives, children, onto the buses to Kladanj. I did not see any either. I knew that they had to register in one house and I understood from Deputy Commander Robert Franken from UNPROFOR, on the 12th, that 35 men were being kept there. What I understood was the overall understanding of the national staff that they were fearing to be killed. And, therefore, I wanted to keep them with me, in order to prevent that happening.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you speak about the fate of the people in Potocari, you are not speaking about the 20-odd thousand who were evacuated to Kladanj. You're not speaking about civilians but, rather, about the 35 who were singled out as suspects or as fighters?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I am not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: Whether you meant the thousands of civilians and their fate when you said the fate of the people in Potocari. What you did mean at that moment; and what did you know about their fate at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: What I knew was the fate of the female and old and children population who were being deported on the buses to Kladanj. That is what I saw. I did not see any male person in that group. I knew that 35 male were kept in that house and that others had [Realtime transcript read in error "as I said"] to register there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Apologies, just a quick correction. I think she just said "and others had to register there." On line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did you first learn about any killings?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I learned about the killings only after I had left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you learn about them? In which way?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I did hear that in -- in the media and from my organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When? Can you remember when it was?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember. It was shortly after I had been back in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were in the countries that made up former Yugoslavia, even in Zagreb, on 22 July, you were still unaware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Schmitz, I'm asking you whether you were aware of the killings on 12 July in Zagreb? Did you have a debriefing then, or possibly a press conference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, is it 12 July or 22nd July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 22nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But previously, Ms. Schmitz, you said: "It was shortly after I had been back in Germany" that you became aware of that killing. But is it consistent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shortly after 22nd July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, whether it -- whether you were aware of the killing before you had gone back to Germany.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of the -- I did not have any proof or information about the killings before arriving in Zagreb on 22nd of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see 65 ter 23109. And it's page 6175. It doesn't have to be broadcast if what I read here is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think they should be under seal. And if we are going to deal with a document that hasn't been dealt with by Ms. West, we will add it to the -- to that bunch of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a cable that you sent on 12 July and which speaks about the evacuation of the wounded and goes on to mention the 35 people who were separated and kept in a room? Is it also true that Mr. Franken, or somebody, informed you that they were being treated well? And this is -- this has to do with what you were saying a minute ago; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes. I have written this telex, and I had gotten the information from Commander Franken. I had never been myself in that house. Your Honour, I am allowed to make an addition to -- to the whole topic of killings because I realise that I had not said something which I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to check in the document whether it is 12th or 13th July. I don't remember exactly that day, but there is a telex, and that I also clearly remember, I don't always, but this I clearly remember was the information from one of the UN soldiers that behind one of the buildings there were dead bodies laying, and if I wanted to have a look at them. I was unsure if that was my task and I was unsure if that was in this rather tense situation safe enough for me to do. So what I did is I asked one of the soldiers of the BSA if he would guarantee my security and he denied that, so I did not go. However, that is one moment where I hear about dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Schmitz.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can this be tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Is this not the document you dealt with -- this will be added.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 6177.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the basis for your suspicion that people would be killed? When did you -- or when were you informed by DutchBat officers that those people would not be killed, as we can see in your cable dated 13 July?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I repeat what I understand. I understand the question as when was I was informed about the fact that Franken and Karremans were sure that nobody of the men would be killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are done with that topic. You said that you learned of the killings soon after your return to Germany, so let's leave it at that. But you said that at that time you were afraid for the persons from your organisation because they might be killed. Why did you think that they might be killed, given the fact that the commanders of DutchBat were -- told you that they would not be killed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Because I did trust my national staff more than the information of UNPROFOR in that moment. And my national staff was extremely worried of getting killed, so I did take that concern very serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be added?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2211, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is part of 23109. So that will be added to the Prosecution Exhibit for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add another information. I'm sorry, I'm a bit nervous. But thinking about this whole theme again, there was one more example which also remained very strong in my memory. Again, which is not a proof but an impression. So on 13th of July, a young Muslim father with a one-year-old child on his arm came towards me being followed by an armed BSA soldier and I did not speak the language. I was with one UN soldier outside at a place where we looked at possible patients, and what he and I understood was that the mother of the child was dead and that the father had nobody to give the child to, and so I agreed to take it and he was being led away by the soldier. And I had a feeling I have to separate the child from the father.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that your understanding was based on the interpretation of somebody who didn't speak Serbian well or, to be more specific, who interpreted for you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: One of the UN soldiers was with me and he understood little. And what he did is writing the name of the child on a paper, Irma, and so the question is why did he give me his daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you later learned that the child was given back to its mother -- to its mother because the mother wasn't dead after all?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the previous page, 6176.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. This is also one of your cables; correct? We see your name at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was on the 12th at 9.10 p.m. [As read] [In English] "... part of the patients have gone to Bratunac with UN. It's a total chaos and UN lets most of its MSF doing." [Interpretation] And a little further down you say: [As read] [In English] "Spoke also briefly with Mladic. I requested him that I could pick up the sick. He agreed." [Interpretation] At least twice you met Mladic, and he granted all your requests; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I met Ratko Mladic twice on the 12th of July. And on the first kind of meeting, that was when I requested that the evacuation of the patients under our care would not be done by BSA towards Bratunac. He did not grant that me, but he told me to do my job and went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you didn't see any bodies or any killings but you did hear sporadic shooting from small weapons? That is, automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I did hear on two -- very clearly on two occasions single shots and that was around the house where the men were supposed to be kept. And on the 13th, late in the evening when it was dark and we had some dinner outside, in the forest, I heard a number of single shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you notice and mention in your cables, or, indeed, your statements, that the Serbian soldiers were celebrating their victory and sowing their wild oats?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the last part of the sentence I did not understand at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that the Serbian soldiers were celebrating their victory and partying and feeling like winners?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this telegram. And here you're saying that the Serbian soldiers were firing shots in the air. Were you familiar with those -- this kind of behaviour in the Balkans, that people fire shots in the air when they celebrate?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder why this information about firing shots in the air cannot be found in your statements, although you were aware of that fact at the time, that they were shooting in the air.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: What would be the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why can we not find that in the statements, in your statements, although we can see it in this cable?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I'm not able to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient, we will take a break now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document also be added?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be also added to the Prosecution exhibit. We admit it as part of associated exhibits. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Ms. Schmitz, that you proposed yourself that the group be reduced to two and that the two of you travelled without any problem?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: It was not myself being present in negotiations before the 24th of June about our journey to Srebrenica, but it was -- it were the colleagues from Paris and Brussels who discussed it. I cannot confirm that we proposed it, or it was asked. We did travel without problems, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that, among other things, you took upon yourself security issues as well and that you attended daily meetings on security?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: It's true that I attended daily security meetings at 10.00 a.m. with, among others, the UN. The first part of the question, please define more clearly what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You described somewhere - and I can find it - your own tasks and competencies as communication with local authorities and personnel and, among other things, security issues; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I also remember where I wrote that, and I'm also -- it is true that this was one of my main tasks. So when I arrived, my priority was to check that everything was in order, like the bunker; like, for example, that I knew how it dismantle the radio and bring it down to the bunker and fix it there again. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us briefly what did those daily security meetings look like? Who attended and what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: We were meeting in the PTT building at 10.00 a.m. every morning. Present was usually the local representative of ICRC, the local representative of UNHCR, one UNMO, United Nations Military Observer, and somebody from the UN, and, of course, myself. And then the UN -- the UNPROFOR member informed about what had happened the day before, and after that, we -- whatever questions came up could be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said, didn't you, that in the early days, when you arrived, the situation was relative quiet?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: In terms of security, the situation was relatively quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You took over from the Red Cross the assessment that there were about 40.000 population. How old was that ICRC assessment?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Did you receive information whether the population was rising or decreasing with time? In other words, did people wish to leave and did they, indeed, leave using UNHCR vehicles?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I did not receive any information between my arrival on 24th of June until 6th of July, that the population figures were rising or decreasing. That was a short period of 12 days. The second part of your question: Did people leave with UNHCR vehicles? Did I understand that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was there any evacuation even before the fall of the enclave, and even if you didn't see it yourself, did you receive information that people were willing to leave, and the Serb army was frequently allowing people to leave on UNHCR trucks.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I do not remember if people left. If people left on UNHCR trucks, for what reason, I do not remember. If it did happen, then before my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You confirmed, didn't you, that the hospital in Potocari was well-equipped?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Is the question that I confirmed that the hospital is well equipped? Then that is based on my usual experience in projects. That is not said that the hospital was well equipped compared with a hospital in Berlin, but, rather, compared with a hospital in other locations, like, for example, I worked in Chechnya before or in Somaliland. So I don't know to which document you are referring and to which equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you give an interview to the French Parliamentary Commission on 29 March 2001?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3 of that interview, you said there had been two medical teams and a well-equipped hospital in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Now the well-equipped hospital I was referring there was the one of UNPROFOR, and the two medical teams were present in the enclave from the 5th of July on, because there was -- the old medical team was supposed to replaced by the new one. The new one arrived on 5th of July. The old one could only leave on 14th of July, due to the events. So that was the reason why there were two medical teams of UNPROFOR in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that comparison from earlier with Berlin related to the civilian hospital in Srebrenica. You didn't mean the UN hospital. You meant the civilian hospital.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes. I -- when you were asking that, I didn't know exactly to what document and telex and saying of myself you were referring, because I as myself did not remember that the hospital in Srebrenica was well equipped. Now I realise that you -- you meant the one in UNPROFOR. So the hospital in Srebrenica, as I said earlier, was equipped, but certainly not as well as a hospital in Berlin but more -- if I compare it with other locations where I have been working in war situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My mistake. When I was saying the hospital in Potocari, I thought we understood it was the UN hospital.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: The hospital in Potocari was the UN hospital. The hospital in Srebrenica was the one of Ministry of Health where we were supporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this one of your first -- no, it's not one of the first, but it's dated 1st July, 1995, this telegram.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, I have here the sitrep of the period 24th of June until 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And first you speak about security. And you say on the 24th of June, Srebrenica was attacked by paramilitaries who had entered through an old tunnel; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that you attended morning briefings on security, was the offensive of Muslim forces from Srebrenica targeting surrounding Serb areas ever mentioned there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I would have to go in -- back into the documents. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said here -- I'll read it: [In English] "... in general, according to the figures and opinion of DutchBat, number of shooting in the enclave and also outside increases. However, number of armed B and H in the streets is decreasing." [Interpretation] Did you receive any explanation where those soldiers from the streets were whose number was dropping?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No, I did not. We did not move much. So personally I do not remember seeing any soldiers in the streets of Srebrenica at the times when we were walking through the streets, which was not often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your telegram?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: This is my telegram. However, what I usually did after the security meetings is that I copied -- the information I had gotten from the UN I copied into the telexes or sitreps in order to send to Belgrade. And so in this one, again, in -- it does say, "according to the figures an opinion of DutchBat," so I'm copying what DutchBat says, but that does not reveal my opinion or my observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, it seems that the next thing that comes up, population condition, is your observation. The usual busy street life, wood cutting everywhere, many children outside. I'll read in read English now. [As read] [In English] "... appear on the first sight well fed and healthy. Also the crowds in front of the ambulantas. Market prices not changed, however, less activities due to the fear of the people." [Interpretation] So your first insight is there are many children in the street and those children appear well fed and healthy; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yeah, that is true. Of course, I do -- I did compare with my experience in other places. Srebrenica was my seventh mission and I had been working mostly in Africa, where, for example, in Liberia I had worked in a famine, where on first sight one can see acute malnourished children. So with that experience I looked in Srebrenica and I didn't see that. So when I look in a project at children, at signs of malnutrition, I see acute malnutrition immediately, but it is difficult for me, due to lack of experience, to see the chronic malnutrition, which is stunting. So if I say that, yes, this is what I observed myself in the first day, then it means I didn't see any acute malnutrition, which is a usual sight in projects of my institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A bit further down you say that you had a long meeting with the opstina, the municipality. And you discussed the hot topics. Could you tell us, what were those hot topics you had to raise with the authorities?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, it's singular, the hot topic, and it was the topic of Mohammed and Meho coming back to work and ending their suspension. Respectively, national staff of my institution having to leave their positions in order to make space for others. That was the hot topic. And given that we were only two, Daniel and myself, and there was no international logistician, and given that I was not a logistician but a nurse in the field, co-ordinator, I definitely needed the national experienced staff to have the mission ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know about the smuggling, the crime, the smuggling of humanitarian aide and medicines, and did you raise such issues with the municipality?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I did not raise any issues with the municipality. I was informed that one examination table had been brought to Zepa. Otherwise, smuggling and crime, you would have to define more. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if you didn't discuss it, it's not necessary. But did you receive information that the town was largely controlled or, if not controlled, largely influenced by a group of criminals? They were smuggling and manipulating with humanitarian aide, smuggling and black marketeering food and medicines. Did anyone inform you about the situation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I was not aware of what you are saying now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see a bit further down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say the convoy entered on the 27th of June. Did you know that, at the time, Muslim forces had long been attacking Serbian villages to facilitate the position of the Muslim army in Sarajevo, and, in the meantime, convoys were still arriving?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Still further down, look at the subheading "Pharmacy/Drugs": [In English] "Certainly a good number of drugs have runned out, but no emergency/case needs to be refused." [Interpretation] Is that also consistent with the situation you noticed and reported?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand the question. Please repeat. That is what I observed, i.e., during that 12 days before the bombing started. However, I did not have the time to -- to sit myself in the pharmacy and look -- and have a closer look towards stocks and amounts and drugs which needed to be ordered, and so on. But that was what I reported. That was what I observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm told -- no, I have ... we have a second page, yes. I see it. Ending with 7329.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We just need it in e-court. 7329.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we looking at 65 ter 23134?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Registrar was ... yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand what the problem is. 65 ter 23134. It's a situation report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it has two pages, not one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem with the Registry's computer. Could you move onto another topic in the meantime. Ms. West, this document hasn't been admitted as an associated exhibit, has it?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It has not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit it as Defence exhibit. We give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2211, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, do you have two pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very strange. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If there's time we'll come back to see the second page. Could we now see from this document, from this collection 23109, page 6137.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this telegram?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your efforts to preserve your objectivity, you also wonder about the mandate of the UNPROFOR and UN CIVPOL; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, I had wanted a clear definition once more from the team in Belgrade -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you help us with the date? I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Then I will have to look it up. Well, I will have to look it up in my papers as well because I don't see the date here either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The previous one was 5 July. This must be the 6th. Towards the bottom, we see the date. It's still 5th July. It's the 5th.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: It's the second page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, second page of the previous page, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is dated 5th July, sent at 1612 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- 24 Why don't we show him the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you say that this mission is a Pandora's Box; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yeah, I did say that. Because we did have -- we were only allowed a two-hour hand-over. Normally, if I take over from somebody, then I have one, two, three, four days. So on 24th of June, I had two hours with my predecessor and then they left. So I did have to discover a lot by myself, and that is why I wrote that it was a Pandora Box.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you got an estimate from Andre that the Serbian army would want to narrow down the enclave; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Are -- are you referring to the same telex? And are you referring to Andre of UNHCR on the 27th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we read under "security" your words, that -- that there are rumours -- "rumour of today," it says. Have you found it?
